desc:
The values in the tree tree are all distinct. The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root down to a leaf (a tree with only a root has height 0).

Each entry of queries is the value of some node other than the root. For every query, imagine removing that node together with its whole subtree from the original tree, and report the height of what is left. The queries are independent: the tree is restored before the next one.

Return an array with one height per query, in the same order.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, -1, 6, 7] (height 3, through 1 → 2 → 4 → 7) and queries = [4, 2, 6, 3] the answer is [2, 2, 3, 3]: removing 4 or 2 cuts the longest path and the next longest has 2 edges, while removing 6 or 3 does not touch it.
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 10,000, and all node values are distinct
The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
Every query is the value of a node of the tree and is not the root's value; queries may repeat
hints: Recomputing the height after every removal costs O(n) per query, which is too slow if both the tree and the number of queries are large. Prepare something once and answer each query in O(1).
Removing a subtree can only lower the height if its node was on the deepest path. Look at nodes on the same level as the removed node: some other node on that level may still lead just as deep.
For each depth d, store the best and second best value of depth + height over all nodes at depth d. Removing node x at depth d leaves max(d - 1, best of its level excluding x).
editorial: Every root-to-leaf path passes through exactly one node on each level it reaches. If x is removed, the deepest remaining node is either reached through another node y at the same depth as x (it then has length depth(y) + height(y)) or it is at most the parent of x, at depth depth(x) - 1. Longer paths avoiding x must also pass through some node at x's depth, unless they are shorter than that depth.

So compute, for every node, its depth and its height (edges down to the deepest leaf) with two passes over the level-order array (forward for depth, backward for height). For each depth keep the two largest values of depth + height together with the node that owns the largest. A query for node x at depth d uses the best value of level d unless that is x itself, in which case it uses the second best (or nothing). The result is max(d - 1, that value).
Preparation is O(n) and every query is O(1). This is the key idea behind many "answer each removal query" tree problems: summarise each level by its top two candidates.
